4538.statement: In the medieval period it was expected that rulers would be ruthless in killing anyone who opposed them.
4538.correction: Rulers were expected to be just and merciful in the medieval period, and Willian faced criticism across Europe for his brutality in crushing opposition in the North of England.

11008.belief: William the Conqueror was hostile towards all Anglo-Saxons from the start.
11008.statement: William the Conqueror was hostile towards all Anglo-Saxons from the start.
11008.correction: Some Anglo-Saxons, if they had not fought against William at Hastings, were allowed to keep their land.

11012.belief: William always planned to replace Anglo-Saxons in key government positions with loyal Normans.
11012.statement: William always planned to replace Anglo-Saxons in key government positions with loyal Normans.
11012.correction: At first, William intended to boost his claim to be the legitimate heir of Edward by keeping earls Edwin, Morcar and Waltheof in place in his government of England - alongside new earls such as Earl Odo of Kent or Earl William of Hereford.

5376.belief: Paying homage, swearing allegiance, or making promises were weak obligations.
5376.statement: Paying homage, swearing allegiance, or making promises were weak obligations.
5376.correction: In fact, these promises are with the king and God. It was unlikely you would break a public and spiritual promise like this; it would not have been good for your reputation or your soul!

11009.belief: William copied the landholding system for Norman England from Normandy.
11009.statement: William copied the landholding system for Norman England from Normandy.
11009.correction: Landholding in Normandy was different from landholding in Norman England. William was not the owner of all the land in Normandy.

5428.belief: People think the survey and Domesday Book are one and the same thing.
5428.statement: People think the survey and Domesday Book are one and the same thing.
5428.correction: In fact, the survey was ordered in 1085, and later compiled into what became known as Domesday Book.

10431.belief: Trial by combat and trial by ordeal were punishments for crimes.
10431.statement: Trial by combat and trial by ordeal were punishments for crimes.
10431.correction: Trial by combat and trial by ordeal were ways of finding out who God judged as being innocent and guilty, though the ordeal was certainly punishing for both parties.

1983.belief: As conquerors, the Normans could make any changes they wanted to.
1983.statement: As conquerors, the Normans could make any changes they wanted to.
1983.correction: The Normans were greatly outnumbered in England and William hoped to convince most English people that his was going to rule in the same way as King Edward the Confessor.

10365.belief: Towns and cities have always been where the richest people in society live.
10365.statement: Towns and cities have always been where the richest people in society live.
10365.correction: For most of English history, the richest people were landowners and lived in the manor house of their manorial estate.

10874.belief: Village life was the same all over Norman England.
10874.statement: Village life was the same all over Norman England.
10874.correction: While there were many common features, the Viking settlement of the Danelaw meant that freemen in villages in the east were much more independent of the lord of their village's manor than in other parts of the country.

4972.correction: The Normans were enthusiastic adopters of Romanesque building style, but it was developed in northern Italy and France, combining Roman features with elements of Byzantine design.

5695.belief: Poor people in medieval England survived by eating potatoes.
5695.statement: Poor people in medieval England survived by eating potatoes.
5695.correction: Potatoes were unknown in Europe until the 16th century.

3093.belief: Forest in Norman England always meant land covered by trees.
3093.statement: That forest in Norman England always meant land covered by trees.
3093.correction: Forest in Norman England meant an area that was reserved for hunting and so could include open land, village land, even towns, as well as woodland.

11010.belief: William I introduced a whole new social system called the feudal system which was completely different from what came before.
11010.statement: William I introduced a whole new social system called the feudal system which was completely different from what came before.
11010.correction: In fact, many of the features of what became known as the feudal system were already in place in Anglo-Saxon England. William took the opportunity to increase his control over society to enable the extraction of wealth; his successors built on this.

5748.belief: The power of the Church in the medieval and modern period is equivalent.
5748.statement: The power of the Church in the medieval and modern period is equivalent.
5748.correction: The medieval Church was a very powerful institution, it was involved in governing Anglo-Saxon England (as bishops served as advisors to kings) and it was a very wealthy landholder. The modern-day Church in England has less powers.

4017.belief: Lanfranc's reforms introduced new concepts like celibacy for monks, Benedictine rules for monasteries and separate courts for the Church (or even archdeacons).
4017.statement: Lanfranc's reforms introduced new concepts like celibacy for monks, Benedictine rules for monasteries and separate courts for the Church (or even archdeacons).
4017.correction: All these were already present in Anglo-Saxon England - monasteries had been following the laws of St Benedict for centuries, for example - but Lanfranc revitalised them, ensured that they were carried out and repurposed them to boost Norman control.

2031.belief: The controversies and conflicts between the crown and the Church were specific to Norman England.
2031.statement: The controversies and conflicts between the crown and the Church were specific to Norman England.
2031.correction: In fact, the controversies and conflicts between the Church and the crown happened in many kingdoms in Europe, and were more severe than in England in particular cases, especially the Holy Roman Empire.

4973.belief: The Normans reforms of the Church were specific to England.
4973.statement: The Normans reforms of the Church were specific to England.
4973.correction: The Church reforms were part of a much bigger European reform movement led by a succession of popes known as the Reform Papacy.

4713.correction: Although individual monks gave up all their possessions, Norman monasteries were often extremely wealthy because they held very large amount of land granted to them by the king or Norman barons and knights.

4967.belief: The Norman conquest was a brutal military occupation which resulted in wholescale change of the English Church.
4967.statement: The Norman conquest was a brutal military occupation which resulted in wholescale change of the English Church.
4967.correction: Whilst there were significant changes, the English Church retained its basic structure and liturgy.

10905.belief: Wales was isolated because of the mountains between Wales and England.
10905.statement: Wales was isolated because of the mountains between Wales and England.
10905.correction: In fact, Wales' extensive coastline meant it had excellent communications with other countries in Europe, especially Ireland.

4969.belief: Before the Norman invasion in 1066, castles were unknown in Anglo-Saxon England.
4969.statement: Before the Norman invasion in 1066, castles were unknown in Anglo-Saxon England.
4969.correction: In fact, Ralph the Timid built a motte-and-bailey castle in Hereford to guard the city against attacks from Wales.

4463.belief: The Marcher earls were completely independent of the king.
4463.statement: The Marcher earls were completely independent of the king.
4463.correction: Although the Marcher earls had a lot of independence and special privileges, they were still vassals of the king and swore to obey him. Their feudal duties included providing the king with knights.

4966.belief: All Norman castles were built to a standard motte-and-bailey design.
4966.statement: All Norman castles were built to a standard motte-and-bailey design.
4966.correction: In fact, although mottes and baileys were features of most Norman castles, how these were positioned could vary a lot, especially if they were built on the site of earlier Roman or Iron Age forts.

9887.belief: The Marcher earls governed their earldoms themselves.
9887.statement: Students may think that the Marcher earls governed their earldoms themselves.
9887.correction: In fact, the Marcher earls were busy men with important matters to deal with in Normandy and England. They appointed deputies, including sheriffs, to govern their earldoms in their absence.

4970.belief: The Norman period in England ended with the death of William I.
4970.statement: The Norman period in England ended with the death of William I.
4970.correction: In fact, there were four more Normans after William I: William II and Henry I (both sons of William I), Matilda (the daughter of Henry I) and Stephen (Henry's nephew). Matilda was not accepted as England's queen, leading to civil war with Stephen.

279.belief: The Anglo-Saxon Church was old-fashioned and corrupt.
279.statement: The Anglo-Saxon Church was old-fashioned and corrupt.
279.correction: The Normans were keen to present the Anglo-Saxon Church that way, but Edward the Confessor had kept up with reforms from the rest of Europe.

8862.belief: There are relatively few sources for Norman England, so historians have less to say about this period than later periods of English history.
8862.statement: There are relatively few sources for Norman England, so historians have less to say about this period than later periods of English history.
8862.correction: Historians have plenty to say about Norman England because they are able to interpret the sources available in many different ways to support many different theories.

9706.statement: Students commonly do not provide enough detail from their historic environment in their answers.
9706.correction: Try to back up your analysis of the question with specific facts and details from your historic environment.

9059.belief: Saints have always been celebrated as they are in modern Britain.
9059.statement: That saints have always been celebrated as they are in modern Britain.
9059.correction: In fact, medieval saints established a cult with many people believing that a prayer close to a saints' relics provided the best chance of help or healing.

4979.belief: Northumbria was an Anglo-Saxon earldom that was fully integrated into the kingdom of England.
4979.statement: Northumbria was an Anglo-Saxon earldom that was fully integrated into the kingdom of England.
4979.correction: Northumbria had a shifting northern border with Scotland and was part of the Danelaw and had different laws and customs from southern England.

677.belief: Bishops have always had a role equivalent to modern times.
677.statement: Bishops have always had a role equivalent to modern times.
677.correction: In fact, bishops in the medieval period were involved in government and even led armies into battle, such as bishop Odo of Bayeux.

885.belief: Cathedrals are like museums and ordinary people can access all areas.
885.statement: Cathedrals are like museums and ordinary people can access all areas.
885.correction: In fact, in medieval times ordinary people could not cross the screen which partitions the nave from the quire.

280.belief: The Anglo-Saxon clergy were not religious.
280.statement: The Anglo-Saxon clergy were not religious.
280.correction: While the Norman reformers viewed many Anglo-Saxon clergy as unsuitable due to their secular lifestyles, this does not mean all were irreligious.

5075.belief: Once a bishop is removed or exiled, they are effectively cancelled from the English nobility forever.
5075.statement: Once a bishop is removed or exiled, they are effectively cancelled from the English nobility forever.
5075.correction: In fact, William Saint Calais and Ranulf Flambard were both restored to their bishoprics after being removed.

285.belief: All Anglo-Saxon prelates (Church leaders) were replaced by Normans.
285.statement: All Anglo-Saxon prelates (Church leaders) were replaced by Normans.
285.correction: Although most bishops and priors were replaced, especially those involved in rebellion, those accused of simony or pluralism and those already married, others were not. The first prior appointed by William St Calais was an Anglo-Saxon called Alwin.

4831.belief: The natural features of England haven't changed much in 1000 years.
4831.statement: The natural features of England haven't changed much in 1000 years.
4831.correction: England has changed enormously in 1000 years! The coastline has shifted so that it would be unrecognisable for a traveller from 1000 years ago, and other natural features, such as The Fens, have shrunk and changed considerably.

8779.belief: There were no real areas of wilderness left in England by the time of the Norman Conquest.
8779.statement: There were no real areas of wilderness left in England by the time of the Norman Conquest.
8779.correction: The population of England in 1066 is generally estimated to have been about two million. The people of England were not evenly spread around the country however, and large parts of the land had no human habitation at all.

4730.belief: Motte-and-bailey castles took years to build.
4730.statement: Motte-and-bailey castles took years to build.
4730.correction: Stone castles could take several years to build; however, the Normans could erect the main defences of a motte-and-bailey castle in as little as a week, usually using large amounts of local labour.

878.correction: Norman castles were effective defensive structures, but they also performed other essential tasks. They were the administrative centre of the local area, the home for the local lord or sheriff and a symbol of Norman power over the Anglo-Saxons.

3961.belief: Kings have always passed on their whole kingdoms to one successor.
3961.statement: Kings have always passed on their whole kingdoms to one successor.
3961.correction: Throughout history, there have been many examples of rulers dividing their lands amongst their sons. Quite frequently, this led to war between the sons in an attempt to reunite the realm.

877.belief: Castles built by the Normans were designed to intimidate the local Anglo-Saxons and provided no benefit for them.
877.statement: Castles built by the Normans were designed to intimidate the local Anglo-Saxons and provided no benefit for them.
877.correction: One of the primary functions of castles was to intimidate the local population, but castles also frequently drew people to them and created an urban centre, which boosted the local economy.

567.belief: The Bayeux Tapestry was created by Franco-Normans in Bayeux.
567.statement: The Bayeux Tapestry was created by Franco-Normans in Bayeux.
567.correction: The Bayeux Tapestry was commissioned by Odo, the Bishop of Bayeux, for Bayeux Cathedral, but historians are now almost certain that it was created in Canterbury by English seamstresses.

3203.belief: The fyrd had low military value because it was made up of untrained peasants.
3203.statement: The fyrd had low military value because it was made up of untrained peasants.
3203.correction: The general fyrd had a lower military value in some contexts (though guarding a coastline might not have been one of them), but the select fyrd meant Anglo-Saxon fyrd armies could include trained and well-equipped men as well.

11011.belief: If William had more knights, he would have won the Battle of Hastings more quickly.
11011.statement: If William had more knights, he would have won the Battle of Hastings more quickly.
11011.correction: Knights may have been less effective against the shield wall than infantry, because the unarmoured horses were vulnerable. They were probably much more effective in later stages of the battle, once the shield wall had been broken up.

3969.belief: We know for sure that William used a feigned retreat tactic at the Battle of Hastings.
3969.statement: We know for sure that William used a feigned retreat tactic at the Battle of Hastings.
3969.correction: In fact, the best sources we have for the battle say different things, for example, that a real retreat gave William the idea of using feigned retreats, or that the 'real' retreat was planned all along.

2687.belief: The English were unprepared for William's invasion.
2687.statement: The English were unprepared for William's invasion.
2687.correction: Harold led detailed preparations for the invasion, with those preparations delivering an army for the Battle of Hastings despite the disbanding of the southern fyrd and the previous formation of two fyrd armies to combat the earlier Viking invasion.

11006.belief: William barons had to do what he said because of feudalism.
11006.statement: William barons had to do what he said because of feudalism.
11006.correction: Feudalism in Normandy was not as strict as it would be in Norman England, and the barons also argued that their promises to obey William were for Normandy - they didn't extend across the Channel to England.

3497.belief: If historians disagree, it means what they are discussing probably never happened.
3497.statement: If historians disagree, it means what they are discussing probably never happened.
3497.correction: Historians disagree about interpretations of an event: instead of historical evidence being about proving something to be true or false, it is much more about how strong the evidence is to support one interpretation over another.

4540.belief: Medieval sources may be biased but the events they record did take place.
4540.statement: Medieval sources may be biased but the events they record did take place.
4540.correction: Medieval sources were influenced by classical authors, and events were often made up to match classical accounts - for example, great events being delayed because the wind was in the wrong direction.

8998.belief: Romanesque buildings only began to be built in England after the Norman Conquest.
8998.statement: Romanesque buildings only began to be built in England after the Norman Conquest.
8998.correction: Edward the Confessor's Westminster Abbey was built in Romanesque style and completed in 1065.

287.belief: Anglo-Saxons did not have castles so therefore their settlements did not have strong fortifications.
287.statement: Anglo-Saxons did not have castles so therefore their settlements did not have strong fortifications.
287.correction: Anglo-Saxon burhs were fortified settlements, surrounded by strong walls designed to deter Vikings from attacking.

9966.belief: The White Tower was the only castle in Norman London.
9966.statement: Students may think that the White Tower was the only castle in Norman London.
9966.correction: In fact, there were two other castles in Norman London: Baynard's Castle and Montfichet's Tower.

4965.belief: All Norman castles were built to the same design.
4965.statement: All Norman castles were built to the same design.
4965.correction: In fact, although we learn about the classic motte-and-bailey castle (and maybe even make models of them in school), there was a very wide variety of castle designs in England and in Normandy.

2542.belief: Early medieval kings ruled from a royal palace.
2542.statement: That early medieval kings ruled from a royal palace.
2542.correction: In fact, early medieval kings and their courts travelled from one location to another.

10996.belief: The White Tower was always bustling with royal activity.
10996.statement: The White Tower was always bustling with royal activity.
10996.correction: Royal residents were seldom present. Most of the time, the White Tower was managed by the keeper and housed a garrison of soldiers.

11014.belief: William I often used the Chapel of St John for his own private worship.
11014.statement: William I often used the Chapel of St John for his own private worship.
11014.correction: Although this was the plan, William died before the chapel was finished.

284.belief: Anglo-Saxon monasteries all followed the same rules, as set out by St Benedict.
284.statement: That Anglo-Saxon monasteries all followed the same rules, as set out by St Benedict.
284.correction: In fact, the abbot of a monastery was able to decide what the rules of their monastery should be, so that there was a lot of variation between monasteries.

8834.belief: All reform in monasteries came from the Cluniac order.
8834.statement: That all reform in monasteries came from the Cluniac order.
8834.correction: In fact, some Benedictine monasteries also introduced reform, and monasteries were reforming in 10th century Anglo-Saxon England well before the Cluniac order arrived in England.

11013.belief: William took land from Anglo-Saxons and gave it to his Norman followers.
11013.statement: William took land from Anglo-Saxons and gave it to his Norman followers.
11013.correction: While William certainly did redistribute land from Anglo-Saxons to Normans, he followed a legal process for this, based on forfeiture - he took the lands of those who did not submit to him as their king, which included those fighting him at Hastings.

9696.belief: Pilgrimages were introduced by the Normans.
9696.statement: Some students may believe that pilgrimages were introduced by the Normans.
9696.correction: Christians have gone on pilgrimages since the 4th century, although the 'golden age' was from the early 11th to the 16th century.

588.belief: Because the priory is so large, it must have been home to many hundreds of monks.
588.statement: Because the priory is so large, it must have been home to many hundreds of monks.
588.correction: In fact, only 20 to 30 monks lived at Castle Acre Priory at any one time, and the original number when the priory was first being built was only around 6.

5821.belief: A priory would only have had a religious function in Norman England.
5821.statement: A priory would only have had a religious function in Norman England.
5821.correction: In fact, the Normans used religion extensively in gaining political, social, cultural and economic control over England.

10872.belief: The Vikings were nothing but brutal savages.
10872.statement: The Vikings were nothing but brutal savages.
10872.correction: Whilst the Viking aptitude for battle is well known, they were also exceptional explorers and traders. Raiding was simply another way for them to gain wealth as opposed to their only way of life.

10871.correction: Whilst Vikings did come from Norway, some of the most problematic Vikings from an English perspective came from Denmark. Vikings also came from Sweden.

2672.belief: England had not been invaded before the Norman Conquest.
2672.statement: England had not been invaded before the Norman Conquest.
2672.correction: Britain had been invaded many times before the Norman Conquest: by the Romans, the tribes known as Angles and Saxons and by the Vikings.

8958.belief: Richard the Lionheart was one of the greatest English kings.
8958.statement: Richard the Lionheart was one of the greatest English kings.
8958.correction: Although he was king of England and was born in England, Richard almost certainly did not consider himself English. He never learnt the language and only spent a maximum of 6 months in England during his 10 year reign; he didn't like the weather.

3562.belief: The Hundred Years' War was a war that was fought continuously for 100 years.
3562.statement: The Hundred Years' War was a war that was fought continuously for 100 years.
3562.correction: The Hundred Years' War lasted for 116 years, but there were many years during this period which saw limited or no fighting. It is better to think of this as a period of heightened animosity in which war was either present or not far off.

2670.belief: England has almost never been conquered.
2670.statement: England has almost never been conquered.
2670.correction: England was conquered repeatedly before and during the medieval period, and was even arguably conquered as late as 1688.

4827.belief: Most of the Native Americans were killed in battle by British colonists.
4827.statement: Most of the Native Americans were killed in battle by British colonists.
4827.correction: Although many Native Americans succumbed to British violence, the overwhelming majority of Native Americans were killed by European diseases, to which they had no natural immunity.

239.belief: The Americans won the War of Independence because they had a better army.
239.statement: The Americans won the War of Independence because they had a better army.
239.correction: For much of the war, the American army was a poorly trained militia. Whilst they fought bravely and Washington proved to be an able general, they received significant support from France and Spain which swung the balance of the conflict.

3549.belief: Huguenots were a separate Protestant denomination from other Protestants in Euope.
3549.statement: Huguenots were a separate Protestant denomination from other Protestants in Euope.
3549.correction: Huguenots were Calvinist Protestants, which was a very common form of Protestantism. The term 'Huguenot' merely means they were Protestants from France.

5555.belief: Plantations are large cash-crop farms found in the Americas.
5555.statement: Plantations are large cash-crop farms found in the Americas.
5555.correction: Cash-crop plantations can be found all over the world, but the first plantations were established in Ireland. Protestants loyal to the monarch were 'planted' in Irish Catholic lands to help establish control of the area.

10984.belief: Westward migration always refers to migration to the Americas.
10984.statement: Westward migration always refers to migration to the Americas.
10984.correction: Westward migration also includes the migration of Protestant settlers from Great Britain to Ulster.

747.belief: The British were the only European power trying to gain control over India.
747.statement: The British were the only European power trying to gain control over India.
747.correction: The British, French and Dutch were all attempting to gain a foothold in India and expand their influence there.

3739.belief: India was totally controlled by the East India Company at the time of the Indian Rebellion in 1857.
3739.statement: India was totally controlled by the East India Company at the time of the Indian Rebellion in 1857.
3739.correction: Two-thirds of India was controlled by the East India Company at the time of the Indian Rebellion in 1857.

2138.belief: Cultural exchange between Britain and India was 'one-way'.
2138.statement: Cultural exchange between Britain and India was 'one-way'.
2138.correction: Cultural exchange between Britain and India moved in both directions, with both countries being permanently changed by the other.

737.belief: Britain and competing European powers met at the Berlin Conference before the scramble for Africa had begun.
737.statement: Britain and competing European powers met at the Berlin Conference before the scramble for Africa had begun.
737.correction: Britain and competing European powers had already been 'scrambling' for Africa for the majority of the 19th century. The Berlin Conference was an attempt to put an end to the fighting between European powers over Africa's land and resources.

890.belief: Cecil Rhodes was Prime Minister of South Africa.
890.statement: Cecil Rhodes was Prime Minister of South Africa.
890.correction: Cecil Rhodes was Prime Minister of the Cape Colony - the British colony in the region of southern Africa.

751.belief: All British sources on imperial expansion were positive.
751.statement: All British sources on imperial expansion were positive.
751.correction: Not all British sources on imperial expansion were positive. There was nuance due to British awareness of the realities of empire. However, British sources are more likely to be positive in outlook regarding British imperial expansion.

4977.belief: All those in Northern Ireland were Protestant and all those elsewhere in Ireland were Catholic.
4977.statement: All those in Northern Ireland were Protestant and all those elsewhere in Ireland were Catholic.
4977.correction: Ireland was predominantly Catholic but there was a population in the north who were predominantly Protestant, who remained part of the UK as Northern Ireland after partition.

3916.belief: Jewish persecution and antisemitism only happened in Europe during the 1930s and 1940s.
3916.statement: Jewish persecution and antisemitism only happened in Europe during the 1930s and 1940s.
3916.correction: Jewish persecution and antisemitism had been happening for thousands of years, with Britain expelling all Jews in 1290, without letting them return for hundreds of years.

4604.belief: Migrants all experience the same hardships and migrated for similar reasons.
4604.statement: Migrants all experience the same hardships and migrated for similar reasons.
4604.correction: Migrants' experiences differed greatly from group to group and from person to person. Motivations amongst migrants also differed, even within particular migrant groups.

750.belief: The British public uniformly supported imperial expansion and wars.
750.statement: The British public uniformly supported imperial expansion and wars.
750.correction: British public opinion was not monolithic; there were varied reactions to imperial policies and military actions, including support, indifference and opposition.

4964.belief: Non-white soldiers and citizens of the Commonwealth played a small role during and after both World Wars.
4964.statement: Non-white soldiers and citizens of the Commonwealth played a small role during and after both World Wars.
4964.correction: Non-white soldiers and citizens of the Commonwealth played a significant role during and after both World Wars.

4620.belief: All migration in this period was voluntary and driven by individual choices.
4620.statement: All migration in this period was voluntary and driven by individual choices.
4620.correction: Not all migrations were voluntary at this time. For instance, indentured labour schemes often coerced individuals into migration under harsh conditions. Additionally, Jewish migration was frequently driven by persecution.

2206.correction: Decolonisation happened in different places at different points throughout the 20th century, for reasons specific to each area's context.

2642.belief: The Empire Windrush brought all Caribbean migrants to Britain.
2642.statement: The Empire Windrush brought all Caribbean migrants to Britain.
2642.correction: The Empire Windrush brought the first group of Caribbean migrants to Britain.

4606.belief: All migrants from Kenya and Uganda during the mid-20th century were of Asian descent.
4606.statement: All migrants from Kenya and Uganda during the mid-20th century were of Asian descent.
4606.correction: Not all migrants from Kenya and Uganda during the mid-20th century were of Asian descent; however, large numbers of them were due to the discrimination they faced in newly-independent Kenya and Uganda.

2920.belief: The Falkland Islands have always been uncontested British territory.
2920.statement: The Falkland Islands have always been uncontested British territory.
2920.correction: There is a complex and prolonged sovereignty dispute with Argentina over the Falkland Islands and there were once historical claims by Spain.

2765.belief: The European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Union (EU) have always been the same entity with identical goals and functions.
2765.statement: The European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Union (EU) have always been the same entity with identical goals and functions.
2765.correction: The evolution from the EEC to the EU over several decades, showing progressively deepening integration. This was not a seamless transition but involved significant changes in scope and objectives.

748.belief: The British Nationality Act of 1948 led to an immediate and easy integration of Commonwealth immigrants into British society.
748.statement: The British Nationality Act of 1948 led to an immediate and easy integration of Commonwealth immigrants into British society
748.correction: Although the British Nationality Act of 1948 allowed Commonwealth citizens to settle in the UK, many immigrants faced significant challenges upon arrival.

8865.belief: Religion was the only medieval explanation for the causes of disease and illness.
8865.statement: Religion was the only medieval explanation for the causes of disease and illness.
8865.correction: Religion was a widespread and commonly used explanation for disease but many other theories were also used including miasma, astrology and the Theory of the Four Humours.

4533.belief: All medieval approaches to treatment and prevention were ineffective.
4533.statement: All medieval approaches to treatment and prevention were ineffective.
4533.correction: Some effective methods, such as the use of mint in herbal remedies, existed but the scientific reason for their health benefits was not understood.

916.belief: There was no change in medieval surgery.
916.statement: There was no change in medieval surgery.
916.correction: New developments did occur, such as the use of opium as an anaesthetic and wine to use against infection, but the impact of these was limited.

4189.belief: There was limited access to medical care in medieval Britain.
4189.statement: There was limited access to medical care in medieval Britain.
4189.correction: Although few people were able to afford physicians, most people were able to turn to other sources of care such as that offered by hospitals, wise people or members of their own family.

3534.belief: Hospitals were locations for people to be cured of their illnesses.
3534.statement: Hospitals were locations for people to be cured of their illnesses.
3534.correction: Christian influences meant that medieval hospitals did not try to cure people's illnesses as this might appear to challenge God's will. Instead spiritual care was prioritised in hospitals.

66.belief: The acceptance of many Islamic medical works also encouraged challenges to Galen in medieval Europe.
66.statement: The acceptance of many Islamic medical works also encouraged challenges to Galen in medieval Europe.
66.correction: Islamic medical works were widely accepted but were ignored where they criticised or encouraged challenges to Galen.

4537.belief: Medieval people were not interested in good personal hygiene.
4537.statement: Medieval people were not interested in good personal hygiene.
4537.correction: Personal hygiene was considered important by most, but access to washing facilities was unequal so levels of personal hygiene differed considerably between different groups of the population, such as nuns and monks and poor residents of towns.

2600.belief: There were no effective responses to the Black Death.
2600.statement: There were no effective responses to the Black Death.
2600.correction: No effective treatments existed in the medieval period but some preventative methods, such as quarantines, could help protect people from plague.

8877.belief: The Renaissance led to widespread acceptance of scientific ideas in medicine.
8877.statement: The Renaissance led to widespread acceptance of scientific ideas in medicine.
8877.correction: Opposition to change from physicians and the limits of new discoveries meant that many ideas about the causes of disease remained unchanged.

2120.belief: Criticisms of bloodletting meant it was practiced less.
2120.statement: Criticisms of bloodletting meant it was practiced less.
2120.correction: Bloodletting and other humoural treatments remained popular and were even used to try and treat King Charles II in 1685.

2053.belief: Corrections to Galen's work were accepted virtually immediately.
2053.statement: Corrections to Galen's work were accepted virtually immediately.
2053.correction: Many medical professionals were reluctant to challenge Galen's works and so new ideas, like those of Vesalius, were not accepted immediately.

2052.belief: Correcting Galen's mistakes led to immediate improvements in medical practices.
2052.statement: Correcting Galen's mistakes led to immediate improvements in medical practices.
2052.correction: Despite Harvey's theory suggesting bloodletting would be dangerous, most physicians continued to recommend the procedure as a common form of treatment.

10424.belief: Treatments in hospitals became significantly more effective as more medical staff were employed there.
10424.statement: Treatments in hospitals became significantly more effective as more medical staff were employed there.
10424.correction: Treatments in most hospitals continued to be based on the incorrect Theory of the Four Humours so unhelpful practices such as bloodletting remained common.

3392.belief: The Great Plague was the last serious plague epidemic because a cure was found.
3392.statement: The Great Plague was the last serious plague epidemic because a cure was found.
3392.correction: No effective cure had been developed to treat plague at the time of the Great Plague.

3920.belief: John Hunter's medical impact was entirely beneficial.
3920.statement: John Hunter's medical impact was entirely beneficial.
3920.correction: Hunter's ideas about venereal disease were incorrect but widespread respect for his expertise meant this mistake wasn't corrected for decades.

3912.belief: Jenner's vaccine became widespread and popular almost immediately.
3912.statement: Jenner's vaccine became widespread and popular almost immediately.
3912.correction: There was considerable opposition to Jenner's smallpox vaccine which delayed widespread use of vaccination in Britain until later in the 19th century.

3244.belief: Germ Theory's accuracy meant that it was immediately accepted in Britain.
3244.statement: Germ Theory's accuracy meant that it was immediately accepted in Britain.
3244.correction: Many doctors still defended spontaneous generation and it took the additional proof provided by Robert Koch's work to convince many that microbes caused disease.

2318.belief: Development of the smallpox vaccine helped scientists to develop vaccines for other diseases.
2318.statement: Development of the smallpox vaccine helped scientists to develop vaccines for other diseases.
2318.correction: It was not understood why the smallpox vaccine worked, so no new vaccines were developed until the last decades of the 19th century.

10068.belief: Surgery continually improved during the 19th century.
10068.statement: Surgery continually improved during the 19th century.
10068.correction: Improvements in anaesthetics led to more invasive surgeries which actually made infection a greater problem in the mid-19th century.

3055.belief: Florence Nightingale encouraged reforms based on her acceptance of Germ Theory.
3055.statement: Florence Nightingale encouraged reforms based on her acceptance of Germ Theory.
3055.correction: A lot of Nightingale's ideas were informed by the idea of miasma and how to protect people from it.

4253.belief: London's new sewage system was built in response to John Snow's findings and recommendations.
4253.statement: London's new sewage system was built in response to John Snow's findings and recommendations.
4253.correction: Snow's work was generally overlooked by officials. Instead, London's new sewers were built in response to the Great Stink of 1858.

3354.belief: The government fully implemented Edwin Chadwick's recommendations.
3354.statement: The government fully implemented Edwin Chadwick's recommendations.
3354.correction: Chadwick's recommendations were included in the 1848 Public Health Act but were not compulsory, so many local authorities ignored them.

4142.belief: Lifestyle factors have only been considered important for a person's health in the modern period.
4142.statement: Lifestyle factors have only been considered important for a person's health in the modern period.
4142.correction: Lifestyle factors like diet have been considered important for many centuries, but before the 20th century this was often based on inaccurate ideas like the Theory of Four Humours.

10650.belief: The use of technology in modern medicine means doctors aren't very involved in making diagnoses.
10650.statement: The use of technology in modern medicine means doctors aren't very involved in making diagnoses.
10650.correction: Technology can help patients to monitor some health conditions themselves but many technologies that help diagnosis require a doctor to operate them or to interpret the information they provide.

212.belief: Alexander Fleming developed penicillin as an antibiotic.
212.statement: Alexander Fleming developed penicillin as an antibiotic.
212.correction: Fleming did not believe penicillin would work as an antibiotic. Florey and Chain developed penicillin as an antibiotic.

227.belief: Alternative medicines were mostly abandoned during the course of the 20th century.
227.statement: Alternative medicines were mostly abandoned during the course of the 20th century.
227.correction: Alternative medicines, including practices like homeopathy and the use of herbal medicines, have remained popular, even in 21st century Britain.

695.belief: Blood transfusions were common before the World Wars.
695.statement: Blood transfusions were common before the World Wars.
695.correction: Blood transfusions were carried out in the 19th century but were not common until after the two World Wars in the 20th century.

15.belief: By 1900, British governments accepted large-scale responsibility for managing public health.
15.statement: By 1900, British governments accepted large-scale responsibility for managing public health.
15.correction: British governments still limited their actions to improve public health by 1900 because of laissez-faire attitudes.

4946.belief: The NHS was the only feature of Britain's welfare state which supported public health.
4946.statement: The NHS was the only feature of Britain's welfare state which supported public health.
4946.correction: The NHS was very important but slum clearance and new house building were also important features of the welfare state which benefitted public health.

10775.belief: Vaccinations have been made compulsory to ensure uptake in modern Britain.
10775.statement: Vaccinations have been made compulsory to ensure uptake in modern Britain.
10775.correction: Vaccinations have been voluntary for people to receive in modern Britain but many have been provided free of charge and their benefits promoted to encourage people.

9378.belief: Smoking is the only cause of lung cancer.
9378.statement: Smoking is the only cause of lung cancer.
9378.correction: Non-smokers can also develop lung cancer. Sometimes this is because of passive smoking, but other causes like air pollution can also be responsible.

10873.belief: All Vikings had the same experience of England, adopting very little of the local culture.
10873.statement: All Vikings had the same experience of England, adopting very little of the local culture.
10873.correction: The Viking experience of England was nuanced, depending on where they settled some experienced great hostility. Some were also able to adopt local Christian practices while maintaining some of their pagan practices.

11180.belief: York only became an important city under Viking rule.
11180.statement: York only became an important city under Viking rule.
11180.correction: York was an important army base under the rule of the Romans, but was also used as a capital city under Anglo-Saxon rule. Its location along important trade routes made it an attractive city to any conqueror.

4974.belief: As the Normans were rulers of England, they had entirely positive experiences and faced no hostility.
4974.statement: As the Normans were rulers of England, they had entirely positive experiences and faced no hostility.
4974.correction: The Normans faced rebellions from Anglo-Saxon communities, but were largely unaffected as these rebellions were brutally put down. However, French monks faced increasingly hostility from English subjects.

3915.belief: All Jewish people who migrated to England worked as moneylenders.
3915.statement: All Jewish people who migrated to England worked as moneylenders.
3915.correction: Not all Jewish migrants took up jobs as moneylenders; many took up other jobs and assimilated into English society.

4612.belief: All migrants workers settled in England to work in the wool trade.
4612.statement: All migrants workers settled in England to work in the wool trade.
4612.correction: Not all migrant workers settled in England to work in the wool trade. Italian bankers are an example of a migrant group who were invited to work as moneylenders, and had very little to do with the English wool trade.

4600.belief: Migrant experiences were dependent solely on when they migrated to England.
4600.statement: Migrant experiences were dependent solely on when they migrated to England.
4600.correction: Migrant experiences were dependent on a variety of factors, this includes when they migrated, the relationship between each migrant group and the authorities and where in England they settled.

8835.belief: The Reformation only led to an increase in the number of Protestant refugees in England.
8835.statement: The Reformation only led to an increase in the number of Protestant refugees in England.
8835.correction: The Reformation eventually led to Puritan rule, under which Jewish migrants were reinvited to England.

5420.belief: All people who migrated to England from Flanders had similar experiences.
5420.statement: All people who migrated to England from Flanders had similar experiences.
5420.correction: Walloon weavers had more positive experiences in Canterbury and were awarded greater freedoms, when compared to Flemish weavers in Sandwich.

185.belief: All African migrants in the early modern period were 'unfree' servants.
185.statement: All African migrants in the early modern period were 'unfree' servants.
185.correction: While many African migrants were 'unfree' servants, there were also free men and women who worked in other jobs - for example, John Blanke and Mary Fillis.

3913.belief: Jewish migrants were invited to England for purely economic reasons, just as they were under the Normans.
3913.statement: Jewish migrants were invited to England for purely economic reasons, just as they were under the Normans.
3913.correction: In the early modern period, the rule of the Puritans meant that Jewish people were invited to England in 1655 for both religious and economic reasons.

3550.belief: Huguenots had to settle in England as it was the only Protestant nation in Europe.
3550.statement: Huguenots had to settle in England as it was the only Protestant nation in Europe.
3550.correction: Huguenots were looking to flee to a safe Protestant nation, and England became the choice for around 50 000 Huguenots as it was known to be more tolerant - not because there were no other nations where Huguenots could settle.

5306.belief: As Palatines were not all Protestant migrants they had entirely negative experiences as migrants in England.
5306.statement: As Palatines were not all Protestant migrants they had entirely negative experiences as migrants in England.
5306.correction: Palatines were initially welcomed and supported, as authorities believed they were Protestant refugees. Their experiences became negative as authorities realised that many were Catholics seeking better economic opportunities.

5892.belief: All Protestant migrants had entirely positive experiences.
5892.statement: All Protestant migrants had entirely positive experiences.
5892.correction: Most Protestant migrants had largely positive experiences in this period, however, there are still examples of Protestants who did not maintain the support of the authorities and the Church, such as the Palatines.

3768.belief: The Industrial Revolution meant that no agricultural work was needed anymore.
3768.statement: The Industrial Revolution meant that no agricultural work was needed anymore.
3768.correction: The Industrial Revolution led to an increase in demand for workers in heavy industries - however, there was still some work in agricultural industries and so not all rural people migrated into towns.

2767.belief: All European migrants can be said to have migrated for similar reasons and therefore had similar experiences.
2767.statement: All European migrants can be said to have migrated for similar reasons and therefore had similar experiences.
2767.correction: While there were some similarities in patterns of migration, the experiences of migrants often depended largely on their religion and their relationship with authorities.

4603.belief: Migrants from the Empire only includes those who travelled from as far as Asia and Africa.
4603.statement: Migrants from the Empire only includes those who travelled from as far as Asia and Africa.
4603.correction: As Ireland did not become part of Britain in 1801, many people considered Ireland a colony and therefore Irish migrants are often treated as migrants from within Britain's empire.

4607.belief: All migrants in Liverpool were from Ireland.
4607.statement: All migrants in Liverpool were from Ireland.
4607.correction: While Irish migrants made up most of the migrant community in Liverpool, there were also a growing number of African and Caribbean sailors who settled in the city.

3914.belief: The Jewish migrants who settled in England in the medieval, early modern and industrial periods all migrated for similar reasons and had similar experiences.
3914.statement: The Jewish migrants who settled in England in the medieval, early modern and industrial periods all migrated for similar reasons and had similar experiences.
3914.correction: In each period, there are marked differences in the reasons for Jewish migration but also in the experiences of Jewish migrants.

4601.belief: All migrants in the 18th and 19th centuries migrated for economic reasons and led successful lives in Britain as a result.
4601.statement: All migrants in the 18th and 19th centuries migrated for economic reasons and led successful lives in Britain as a result.
4601.correction: Although most migrants settled for economic reasons, the expansion of the British Empire and greater civil liberties also attracted a greater number of migrants in this period.

1759.belief: Colonial soldiers joined the British war effort in both world wars, out of a sense of nationalism and pride for their 'motherland'.
1759.statement: Colonial soldiers joined the British war effort in both world wars, out of a sense of nationalism and pride for their 'motherland'.
1759.correction: Colonial soldiers had often already been part of standing armies that were ordered to join the war effort, and by 1939 many colonial soldiers were only fighting in the hope that it might win them independence from the British Empire.

4609.belief: All migrants from predominantly white nations were welcomed by authorities and local communities.
4609.statement: All migrants from predominantly white nations were welcomed by authorities and local communities.
4609.correction: Although Irish migrants were encouraged to migrate, they often faced hostility on arriving in Britain. Like Caribbean migrants, many struggled to find suitable accommodation as landlords were unwilling to rent to them.

2649.belief: The end of the British Empire and the growth of the Commonwealth led to increasing migration from the Commonwealth throughout the second half of the 20th century.
2649.statement: The end of the British Empire and the growth of the Commonwealth led to increasing migration from the Commonwealth throughout the second half of the 20th century.
2649.correction: Although migration to Britain initially increased in the second part of the 20th century, it was limited by immigration laws introduced in the 1960s - which aimed to target black and Asian migrants.

8738.belief: The Race Relations Acts completely addressed the issues of racism that were rampant in post-war Britain.
8738.statement: The Race Relations Acts completely addressed the issues of racism that were rampant in post-war Britain.
8738.correction: The Race Relations Act went a long way in showing changing government attitudes and providing some protection to black and Asian people in post-war Britain - but they could not and did not change public attitudes overnight.

743.belief: Britain joined the EU with the intention of encouraging greater migration from Europe.
743.statement: Britain joined the EU with the intention of encouraging greater migration from Europe.
743.correction: When Britain joined the EU in 1973, it was primarily for economic reasons as they hoped to boost their economy through trading relationships with Europe.

8840.belief: Refugees were more welcome than other migrants as Britain wanted to support the idea that they were a liberal and tolerant nation.
8840.statement: Refugees were more welcome than other migrants as Britain wanted to support the idea that they were a liberal and tolerant nation.
8840.correction: Refugees were sometimes more welcome than other migrants. The British government was often careful with their criteria for who was classed as a refugee and, from the 1990s, introduced a number of laws to restrict access to Britain for refugees.

10571.belief: Only the USA had a black civil rights movement.
10571.statement: That only the USA had a black civil rights movement.
10571.correction: Britain also experienced its own civil rights movement; it is often thought to have begun with the Bristol Bus Boycott in June 1963.

10992.belief: All white migrants had positive experiences in the modern period.
10992.statement: All white migrants had positive experiences in the modern period.
10992.correction: Although they were often favoured by immigration laws, they still faced hostility on arriving in Britain. For example, many Irish migrants experienced the same discrimination from landlords as Caribbean migrants.

493.belief: Attempts to prevent infections during surgery mainly focused mainly on antiseptic methods by the start of the 20th century.
493.statement: Attempts to prevent infections during surgery mainly focused mainly on antiseptic methods by the start of the 20th century.
493.correction: Antiseptic methods remained in use but methods of aseptic surgery were also commonly practiced by the start of the 20th century to prevent infections.

4241.belief: The local environment on the Western Front had no significance for medicine and the health of British forces.
4241.statement: The local environment on the Western Front had no significance for medicine and the health of British forces.
4241.correction: Waterlogged and muddy ground threatened soldiers and slowed down medical evacuations whilst bacteria in the local soil created a serious risk of infections.

5676.belief: Poisonous gas was amongst the deadliest weapons used against British soldiers during WWI.
5676.statement: Poisonous gas was amongst the deadliest weapons used against British soldiers during WWI.
5676.correction: Gas attacks accounted for only 1% of deaths amongst British soldiers during WWI.

10069.belief: Most surgical treatment was provided at Base Hospitals.
10069.statement: Most surgical treatment was provided at Base Hospitals.
10069.correction: Most surgeries occurred at Casualty Clearing Stations due to the need to attend to wounded soldiers' needs quickly.

5369.belief: Patients with the most severe wounds were prioritised for operations at CCSs.
5369.statement: Patients with the most severe wounds were prioritised for operations at CCSs.
5369.correction: Patients with the most severe wounds who were unlikely to survive were sent to moribund wards rather than being operated on at CCSs.

337.belief: Antiseptics developed before WWI were able to sterilise wounds against infections like gas gangrene.
337.statement: Antiseptics developed before WWI were able to sterilise wounds against infections like gas gangrene.
337.correction: Antiseptics such as carbolic acid could destroy some bacteria, but had no effect on those which caused gas gangrene. The sodium hypochlorite solution used in the Carrel-Dakin method could destroy the bacteria which caused gas gangrene though.

9697.belief: There was only rationing in Britain during WW2.
9697.statement: Students may believe that there was only rationing in Britain during WW2.

6884.statement: Pupils are likely to be unaware that laws protecting UK citizens against discrimination did not start until mid-60s.
6884.correction: Prior to the Race Relations Act 1965, it was possible to discriminate against black people, for example, refuse to serve them. This was extended in 1968 to include discrimination in housing and education.

2411.belief: The discrimination and exclusion from opportunities that migrants sometimes face is just something these communities have to accept.
2411.statement: The discrimination and exclusion from opportunities that migrants sometimes face is just something these communities have to accept.
2411.correction: In fact, migrants set up self-help schemes and organise their own resources to ensure discrimination and lack of government help do not hold back their community and especially their children's access to opportunities.

9687.belief: Fascism was only a factor in Nazi Germany, and be unaware of the existence of fascist groups in Britain.
9687.statement: Students might believe that fascism was only a factor in Nazi Germany, and be unaware of the existence of fascist groups in Britain.
9687.correction: Fascism spread across Europe in the 1930s, including to Britain, although Britain's strong democratic tradition meant it did not take hold as it did in other countries at the time.

9768.statement: Students may not make the connection between the civil rights movement in the USA and the efforts of black activists in the UK in the 1960s.
9768.correction: Explain to students that the influence of Martin Luther King Jr and Malcolm X spread outside of America.

9735.statement: Students might fail to see the significance of the admission by the police that they acted with racist prejudice.
9735.correction: This was the first time the police had admitted to treating the black community unfairly and was a turning point in the development of civil rights.

9457.belief: If a source has a limitation then it is not reliable or useful for a historical study.
9457.statement: If a source has a limitation then it is not reliable or useful for a historical study.
9457.correction: All sources have limitations as well as strengths, which historians take account of, and does not mean that the source should not be used by a historian.

9752.statement: Students can forget to use the sources provided, and instead simply rely on their own knowledge.
9752.correction: The historical environment questions are mainly source-based and therefore students should base their answers on the sources, using their knowledge to explain what is in the sources and to judge the utility of the sources.

8994.belief: Roles were fixed in Anglo-Saxon society - a peasant would always be a peasant.
8994.statement: Roles were fixed in Anglo-Saxon society - a peasant would always be a peasant.
8994.correction: Anglo-Saxon society was more open to social mobility: a hard-working peasant could gain more land and become a thegn, some slaves became free and an earl could even become king!

2671.belief: England did not have any fortified settlements until the Normans built castles.
2671.statement: England did not have any fortified settlements until the Normans built castles.
2671.correction: In fact, Anglo-Saxon burhs were fortified settlements, built to protect towns from Viking attacks.

1664.belief: Church leaders had no role in how Anglo-Saxon England was governed.
1664.statement: Church leaders had no role in how Anglo-Saxon England was governed.
1664.correction: Archbishops, bishops and other Church leaders could be part of the Witan, and that meant they were involved in advising the monarch about the government of Anglo-Saxon England.

281.belief: An Anglo-Saxon monarch held all the power in their kingdom.
281.statement: An Anglo-Saxon monarch held all the power in their kingdom.
281.correction: In fact, Anglo-Saxon nobles could force their monarchs to do things they did not want to do. For example, King Edward was forced to allow the House of Godwin back from exile and restore them to their earldoms.

3457.belief: Harold Godwinson would help his brother Tostig.
3457.statement: Harold Godwinson would help his brother Tostig.
3457.correction: Harold’s ambitions to be king meant he did little to help his brother Tostig. If Harold became king, he would want to avoid making enemies of Mercia and Northumbria. He wanted to show the Witan that he was loyal to England, beyond his family.

11015.belief: William always used violence to control England.
11015.statement: William always used violence to control England.
11015.correction: Although violence was a recurring tactic of William's, he also allowed some Anglo-Saxons to keep some of their land and was willing to negotiate and pay the Danes to leave England.

4971.belief: The Normans destroyed all Anglo-Saxon government.
4971.statement: That the Normans destroyed all Anglo-Saxon government.
4971.correction: Anglo-Saxon government systems were sophisticated, perhaps more developed than Normandy’s. The Normans retained and built on the existing Anglo-Saxon governmental institutions.

2673.belief: England’s monarchs always spoke English as their first language.
2673.statement: England’s monarchs always spoke English as their first language.
2673.correction: In fact, after the Norman conquest it would take over 300 years for the monarch of England to speak English as their first language.

72.belief: According to the Bayeux Tapestry, Odo played an important role in the Norman invasion.
72.statement: According to the Bayeux Tapestry, Odo played an important role in the Norman invasion.
72.correction: There is reason to be sceptical about this depiction. The Bayeux Tapestry was commissioned by Odo. This perhaps explains why Odo is self-importantly shown as central to the planning and delivery of the invasion.

5126.belief: The one-dimensional view of William as a violent conqueror.
5126.statement: The one-dimensional view of William as a violent conqueror.
5126.correction: In fact, William was very pious and he repented some of the atrocities he had committed during his reign and insisted his treasures should be used to rebuild some of the areas he had harried.

3283.belief: Germany has always existed as one country, or has existed in its current form for a long time.
3283.statement: Germany has always existed as one country, or has existed in its current form for a long time.
3283.correction: Before 1871, 'Germany' did not exist as a single nation. It was a collection of over 30 independent, mostly German-speaking states, each with its own ruler.

9523.belief: The SPD had genuine power after becoming the largest party in the Reichstag.
9523.statement: The SPD had genuine power after becoming the largest party in the Reichstag.
9523.correction: The Reichstag could debate and vote on budgets, but the Kaiser chose the chancellor, controlled the military and could close the Reichstag at will. Foreign and military policy stayed entirely in his hands, so real political power never shifted.

3942.belief: The Kaiser could simply order naval expansion without resistance.
3942.statement: The Kaiser could simply order naval expansion without resistance.
3942.correction: In reality, the Kaiser needed Reichstag approval for funding, so winning public support was a crucial step in pressuring parliament.

3284.belief: Germany formally lost the First World War in the traditional sense, with a decisive military defeat.
3284.statement: Germany formally lost the First World War in the traditional sense, with a decisive military defeat.
3284.correction: Germany was not defeated in battle, it sought peace and agreed to an armistice. The German military leadership recognised that the war was unwinnable due to resource shortages, economic collapse, and the deteriorating morale of troops and citizens.

5884.belief: Proportional representation was purely a positive step forward because it gave a voice to smaller political parties.
5884.statement: Proportional representation was purely a positive step forward because it gave a voice to smaller political parties.
5884.correction: In fact, proportional representation led to fragmentation, with many small parties gaining seats in the Reichstag. This made it difficult to pass laws because no single party had a majority.

603.belief: The belief that the 'stab-in-the-back' theory was based on factual evidence.
603.statement: The belief that the 'stab-in-the-back' theory was based on factual evidence.
603.correction: The theory was a narrative promoted by the military elite to distance themselves from the Armistice surrender. Germany's defeat was primarily due to military exhaustion and economic collapse, not treachery by Weimar politicians.

10974.belief: The Weimar Republic’s reliance on the Freikorps might suggest that the government supported right-wing ideologies.
10974.statement: The Weimar Republic’s reliance on the Freikorps might suggest that the government supported right-wing ideologies.
10974.correction: The Weimar Government used the Freikorps out of desperation to suppress left-wing uprisings, but this reliance highlighted its inability to maintain order independently, rather than an alignment with right-wing ideologies.

3567.correction: Some people, like businessmen who hoarded essentials to sell at inflated prices, profited during the crisis. Meanwhile, many middle-class Germans saw their savings wiped out and were forced to barter for survival.

3285.belief: Germany's recovery in the 1920s completely solved its economic problems and secured long-term stability.
3285.statement: Germany's recovery in the 1920s completely solved its economic problems and secured long-term stability.
3285.correction: Much of the recovery depended on American loans. What happens to Germany’s economy if those loans are withdrawn or if the US faces its own crisis? This shows how fragile the recovery really was.

3946.belief: The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 was a legally binding agreement that could prevent all future wars.
3946.statement: The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 was a legally binding agreement that could prevent all future wars.
3946.correction: The pact lacked enforcement mechanisms and relied on goodwill, making it more symbolic than practical.

10972.belief: Weimar Germany was a completely free and modernist society.
10972.statement: Weimar Germany was a completely free and modernist society.
10972.correction: While it was a hub of cultural experimentation, it was also deeply divided, with strong conservative resistance and widespread political unrest. Many Germans viewed the cultural changes as dangerous and sought to restore traditional values.

8339.belief: Most unemployed Germans turned to communism.
8339.statement: Pupils may think that most unemployed Germans turned to communism.
8339.correction: While the Communist Party gained support, many Germans, especially the middle class and business owners, feared communism and instead supported the Nazis as a defence against a potential revolution.

4846.belief: The Nazis only gained power through fear and intimidation.
4846.statement: The Nazis only gained power through fear and intimidation.
4846.correction: In reality, while violence played a role, their rise was also driven by economic despair, propaganda, Hitler’s appeal, and democratic failures. Many Germans voted for them willingly, believing they offered hope and stability.

5410.belief: People “should have known” what Hitler would do once in power.
5410.statement: People “should have known” what Hitler would do once in power.
5410.correction: In reality, many elites and citizens saw the Nazis as a lesser evil amid crisis — not as future dictators. The horror of what was to come wasn’t yet clear to them.

2647.belief: The Enabling Act was passed fairly.
2647.statement: The Enabling Act was passed fairly.
2647.correction: The vote was deeply manipulated: communist Reichstag members were banned, others intimidated.

3509.belief: Hitler was already an all-powerful dictator by 1934.
3509.statement: Hitler was already an all-powerful dictator by 1934.
3509.correction: While Hitler had crushed political opposition, the military remained a powerful, independent force. The SA purge was crucial to win over the army, which still had the power to challenge him.

5975.belief: All concentration camps in this period were death camps like Auschwitz.
5975.statement: Pupils may assume that all concentration camps in this period were death camps like Auschwitz.
5975.correction: Emphasise that early camps (1933–1939) were brutal prisons for political opponents and ‘undesirables’, but were not yet part of a systematic extermination programme. The Holocaust’s industrial death camps came later.

8867.belief: All religious leaders opposed the Nazis.
8867.statement: All religious leaders opposed the Nazis.
8867.correction: In reality, many remained silent or even cooperated, hoping to protect their institutions.

2802.belief: Everyone in Germany fully believed the Nazi propaganda.
2802.statement: Everyone in Germany fully believed the Nazi propaganda.
2802.correction: While some people genuinely believed, many conformed due to fear, peer pressure, or habit. Propaganda created surface unity - not universal belief.

3282.belief: Most Germans strongly supported the Nazis.
3282.statement: Most Germans strongly supported the Nazis.
3282.correction: Many complied out of fear, peer pressure, or survival - not necessarily belief. Resistance was dangerous, but still present in different forms across society.

11048.correction: Women's experiences under Nazi rule varied: some embraced traditional roles and rewards, while others resisted and faced punishment, showing a complex, not uniform, response to Nazi policies.

9973.belief: All youth blindly accepted Nazi ideas.
9973.statement: Students may think all youth blindly accepted Nazi ideas.
9973.correction: While many participated, some - like Sophie Scholl - resisted. Peer pressure, fear, and excitement all played a role.

4845.belief: The Nazis completely solved unemployment and revived the economy.
4845.statement: The Nazis completely solved unemployment and revived the economy.
4845.correction: While official unemployment figures dropped dramatically, some of this was due to manipulated statistics and forced labour schemes.

2794.belief: Everyone benefited from Nazi economic policies.
2794.statement: Everyone benefited from Nazi economic policies.
2794.correction: Reinforce that benefits were selective, often dependent on loyalty, and many gains were cancelled out by longer hours and lost freedoms.

9689.belief: Germany fully mobilised its population, including women, like the Allies did.
9689.statement: Students may believe Germany fully mobilised its population, including women, like the Allies did.
9689.correction: Nazi ideology restricted women's roles in industry, despite labour shortages.

4844.belief: Nazi concentration camps and extermination camps were the same thing.
4844.statement: Nazi concentration camps and extermination camps were the same thing.
4844.correction: Concentration camps were used for imprisonment, forced labour and punishment, not initially for mass murder. Extermination camps, built later, were designed specifically for killing on an industrial scale.

3510.correction: Antisemitism had deep roots across Europe and the wider world long before Hitler. The Nazis built on these longstanding prejudices, turning them into official state policy and using them to justify persecution.

2990.belief: The Final Solution was decided all at once.
2990.statement: The Final Solution was decided all at once.
2990.correction: It was an evolving process. Historians have debated whether genocide was inevitable from 1933 — policies escalated over time, with many historians seeing Wannsee as marking the coordination point, not the start.

9668.belief: Only businesses benefitted from the boom.
9668.statement: Students assume that only businesses benefitted from the boom.
9668.correction: Consumers benefitted from the boom through increased employment, rising wages, and the ease of buying goods which improved standards of life.

623.belief: The benefits of mass production in the car industry were felt equally by all groups.
623.statement: The benefits of mass production in the car industry were felt equally by all groups.
623.correction: Mass production benefited consumers and businesses greatly but workers suffered from monotonous work and restrictions on trade unionism.

4305.belief: Losers were only those who belonged to minority groups who suffered because of racism.
4305.statement: Losers were only those who belonged to minority groups who suffered because of racism.
4305.correction: Economic problems made life difficult for many people aside from racist issues. These issues affected minorities and non-minorities.

10975.belief: There were well-developed plans for anarchists and communists to stage a revolution in the USA.
10975.statement: There were well-developed plans for anarchists and communists to stage a revolution in the USA.
10975.correction: Although the fear of 'Reds' was widespread, the failure of the Palmer Raids revealed that there were no real plans in place for a revolution which could threaten the USA.

8739.belief: Racial tension was only an issue for African Americans in the 1920s.
8739.statement: Racial tension was only an issue for African Americans in the 1920s.
8739.correction: In both the North and South, Catholics, Jews and recently arrived immigrants frequently experienced prejudice, discrimination and even violence from WASPs, just as African Americans did.

5856.belief: Prohibition led to a fall in alcohol consumption in the USA.
5856.statement: Prohibition led to a fall in alcohol consumption in the USA.
5856.correction: A rise in the number of bars and alcohol-related offences after 1920 suggests that drinking became more common during the Prohibition era.

11051.belief: All women in the USA experienced changes in the same way during the 1920s.
11051.statement: All women in the USA experienced changes in the same way during the 1920s.
11051.correction: The ways in which women experienced changes often differed depending on factors such as race, wealth and location.

4627.belief: Minority groups only experienced hardship as a result of discrimination.
4627.statement: Minority groups only experienced hardship as a result of discrimination.
4627.correction: Some groups such as African Americans experienced economic hardship because of broader structural changes - especially the decline of American agriculture which hurt the South where most African Americans lived.

9252.belief: Only shareholders and speculators lost out from the Wall Street Crash.
9252.statement: Only shareholders and speculators lost out from the Wall Street Crash.
9252.correction: Once speculators went bankrupt, they were unable to repay their debts to banks causing them to fail. Bank failures wiped out the savings of millions of Americans.

237.belief: All Americans were affected in the same way by the Great Depression.
237.statement: All Americans were affected in the same way by the Great Depression.
237.correction: Some issues experienced during the Great Depression differed between rural and urban areas. African Americans also tended to suffer more, with higher rates of unemployment than average.

5789.belief: President Hoover did nothing to try and help Americans during the Great Depression.
5789.statement: President Hoover did nothing to try and help Americans during the Great Depression.
5789.correction: At times, Hoover refused to act to provide relief, especially at the start of the Great Depression, but by 1932, the president was taking more action to try and help, such as setting up the Reconstruction Finance Corporation.

3415.belief: All groups in America experienced increased hardship as a result of the Great Depression.
3415.statement: All groups in America experienced increased hardship as a result of the Great Depression.
3415.correction: Increased hardship was the most common experience during the Great Depression but there still gains for some groups: overall female employment increased and some Americans, such as Hollywood stars, were still able to become very wealthy.

3061.belief: The only focus of the New Deal was to create new jobs and reduce unemployment.
3061.statement: The only focus of the New Deal was to create new jobs and reduce unemployment.
3061.correction: Relief and reform were also important aims of the New Deal. Major policies like the Emergency Banking Act and Social Security Act were more concerned with reform and relief, respectively, than job creation.

8785.belief: The only reason people opposed the New Deal was because it increased costs for the rich and wealthy.
8785.statement: The only reason people opposed the New Deal was because it increased costs for the rich and wealthy.
8785.correction: Radical opposition to the New Deal was based on the idea that it did not do enough to help the poor. Opposition from the Supreme Court was based on judgements that some aspects of the New Deal were unconstitutional.

3390.belief: During the Great Depression, Americans had significantly less access to entertainment.
3390.statement: During the Great Depression, Americans had significantly less access to entertainment.
3390.correction: Americans continued to access entertainments on a large scale. Radio ownership doubled, cinema attendance recovered as a form of escapism and new forms of popular literature like comics flourished.

2579.belief: The economic impacts of wartime production were confined to weapons manufacturers.
2579.statement: The economic impacts of wartime production were confined to weapons manufacturers.
2579.correction: Wartime demand extended to a wide range of goods including weapons, foodstuffs, fuel and raw materials. This led to many sectors of the US economy benefitting from wartime production.

3669.belief: Improved working opportunities for women and African Americans represented an end to discrimination against them.
3669.statement: Improved working opportunities for women and African Americans represented an end to discrimination against them.
3669.correction: African Americans and women continued to face discrimination in the workplace. Women entered 'male' jobs but were paid less than men and many employers still hired disproportionately low numbers of African Americans.

624.belief: The benefits of WW2 were experienced evenly by all groups of Americans.
624.statement: The benefits of WW2 were experienced evenly by all groups of Americans.
